books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 2, 1848, Articles IX and XII (ratified text). Public domain.
stimulus.text: The Mexicans who, in the territories aforesaid, shall not preserve the character of citizens of the Mexican Republic... shall be incorporated into the Union of the United States, and be admitted at the proper time (to be judged of by the Congress of the United States) to the enjoyment of all the rights of citizens of the United States... In consideration of the extension acquired by the boundaries of the United States, as defined in the fifth article of the present treaty, the Government of the United States engages to pay to that of the Mexican Republic the sum of fifteen millions of dollars.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 2, 1848, Articles IX and XII, public domain
stem: The treaty's promise that Mexicans in the ceded territories would be “incorporated into the Union” most directly raised which question for the United States?

options.text: Whether Mexico would pay the United States for the war.
options.misconception: The treaty had the United States paying Mexico $15 million, not the reverse.

options.text: Whether Britain would accept the Oregon boundary.
options.misconception: The Oregon boundary was settled with Britain in 1846, two years before this treaty.

options.text: Whether gold would be found in California.
options.misconception: Gold was found in January 1848, before the treaty was signed; the treaty's promise is about people, not gold.

options.text: Whether the new citizens would be treated equally under American law.

rationales.A: The treaty made the United States pay Mexico $15 million, not the other way around.
rationales.B: The Oregon boundary was settled by treaty with Britain in 1846; this treaty is with Mexico.
rationales.C: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in January 1848, before the treaty was signed in February; the promise concerns people, not gold.
rationales.D: The treaty promised Mexicans in the ceded lands the rights of American citizens — but Congress would judge the timing, and in practice those rights were often denied. Background: the Senate had struck out the original Article X, which would have protected Mexican land grants more firmly.
rationales.general:
1. Read the promise. Mexicans who stayed would be “incorporated into the Union” and enjoy “all the rights of citizens of the United States.”
2. Read the catch. Admission would come “at the proper time (to be judged of by the Congress of the United States).”
3. Ask what that leaves open. Congress controlled the timing, and equal treatment was promised on paper, not guaranteed in practice.
Remember: a treaty's words are a promise, not a result. Ask who decides when the promise is kept — here, Congress did.
